From **August 2009 to June 2012**, Matt served as Technology Delivery Lead for ACCESS Next Generation, the bank’s unified corporate banking portal. The starting point was fragmented: regional payment systems had different data models, client configurations, message formats, and compliance requirements. Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform provided the foundation, but the bank needed payment capabilities and controls well beyond its out-of-box offering.

Matt managed a blended team of **40+** **Accenture** and bank resources across the US, Mumbai, and Bangalore. He spent **70 to 80%** of his time embedded at Bottomline’s Portsmouth offices, managing the boundary between native platform capabilities and bank-specific engineering.

Alongside the payment engine, Matt designed the centralized gateway handling message transformation, protocol translation, and routing across **12 countries**. Corporate treasurers gained a single entry point for wire, ACH, and cross-border transfers rather than separate regional logins.

The supporting work included replacing individual permission configuration with role-based profiles and bulk changes, reducing entitlement management from **days to minutes**. Matt also led payments data migration without disruption to live payment operations, preserving client configurations, entitlements, transaction histories, and compliance traceability. For the regional rollout, he translated local regulatory requirements into data visibility and access controls, sequencing launches by regulatory readiness.

ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, consolidating regional systems into a portal serving **135,000+** corporations, financial institutions, governments, and municipalities across **180+ countries**. The regional compliance framework enabled launches across APAC, EMEA, and the Americas without regulatory blockers.

🐾 Here’s what Matt has built, changed, and delivered.

Matt’s work spans Execution & Delivery, Org & Working-Model Transformation, and Talent & Enablement. He built enterprise platforms, recovered troubled programs, and then built the organization that delivered them: **Accenture’s** Atlanta and Tampa Cloud Innovation Centers, growing from **0 to 150+ practitioners**.

Clients were struggling with slow development cycles, fragmented workflows, and legacy systems. Many new hires lacked hands-on experience with cloud-native technologies or modern engineering practices. Matt brought product managers, designers, and engineers together in balanced teams. He established pair programming, test-driven development, automated delivery pipelines, and customer journey-led development instead of siloed handoffs and a separate testing phase.

When those practices were not working, he addressed the failure directly. At **Norfolk Southern**, defects were rising despite near-complete test coverage. Matt took ownership in front of the client and account leadership rather than defending the dashboard. He audited the code and tests, found tests written after the code and backlog stories without defined scenarios, and rebuilt the backlog with testable stories. He brought in frontend and backend TDD experts to work alongside engineers through coding katas and an “I do, we do, you do” progression. The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see.

That same guided-to-independent learning model helped new CIC practitioners deliver without ongoing oversight. The talent program achieved near-zero attrition in its first **2 years**, with multiple hires promoted.

Across the CIC practice, **10-person** balanced teams delivered equivalent output to traditional **20-person** teams, with **4X faster velocity** and zero-defect deployments. At **JP Morgan Chase**, payments and Salesforce platforms each rolled out across **12 countries**. The Atlanta and Tampa centers delivered **30+ product engagements** across **15+ Fortune 500 clients**, contributing to **\$100M+ in repeat business** through delivery excellence and client relationships.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s a time Matt took accountability for a failure.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization delivery for a financial services client. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production environments. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with existing documentation.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup, but he relied on assumptions rather than verifying the IAM configuration and downstream access controls. He focused on delivery pressures, did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, and did not verify whether production customer names and email addresses had been masked or scrubbed. He also had not implemented compensating controls such as data masking or email interception.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT containing unmasked production customer data. It sent communications to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. They worked collectively to understand what happened and implement corrective controls. The root causes were insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed from downstream environments.

The client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described it as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence,” reinforcing his belief that leaders own the environment their teams operate in.

His stated lesson was that “assumptions are risks in disguise.” IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach.

🐾 Here’s a time Matt took accountability for a failure.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization delivery for a financial services client. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production environments. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with existing documentation.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup, but he relied on assumptions rather than verifying the IAM configuration and downstream access controls. He focused on delivery pressures, did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, and did not verify whether production customer names and email addresses had been masked or scrubbed. He also had not implemented compensating controls such as data masking or email interception.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT containing unmasked production customer data. It sent communications to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. They worked collectively to understand what happened and implement corrective controls. The root causes were insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed from downstream environments.

The client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described it as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence,” reinforcing his belief that leaders own the environment their teams operate in.

His stated lesson was that “assumptions are risks in disguise.” IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach.

🐾 Here’s how Matt built AWS Launchpad.

At **Accenture’s** Liquid Studio, traditional training programs couldn’t keep pace with rapidly evolving AWS technologies. Engineers had gaps in cloud competency, and cloud adoption was slowing. The Atlanta Innovation Hub needed a structured program that would help engineers earn certifications and apply cloud-native technologies on projects.

As Cloud Native Architecture Lead, Matt led AWS Launchpad from **July 2018 to November 2019**, working in collaboration with AWS to develop a tailored enablement program. He designed structured learning paths and certification programs covering AWS core services, including Lambda, API Gateway, DynamoDB, Kubernetes, and ECS/Fargate, alongside cloud-native application development.

Rather than relying on theory alone, Matt delivered interactive workshops and hands-on labs that immersed engineers in real-world AWS environments. He established cloud expert mentorship teams so participants could learn best practices from experienced practitioners. Group coaching sessions and knowledge-sharing workshops gave engineers additional opportunities to work through questions and learn together.

The program combined a defined learning path, practical application, and ongoing mentorship. Its scope extended across **Accenture**, with engineers preparing for AWS Solutions Architect and DevOps Engineer certifications while building the cloud competencies needed for transformation projects.

More than **200 professionals earned AWS certifications** through the program. AWS Launchpad accelerated cloud adoption and the launch of cloud-native initiatives, while the mentorship teams and knowledge-sharing workshops supported continued learning beyond certification.
